\chapter{Why, and Because}
\label{ch:ta-why-and-because}
\hlchaptermodality{78}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for a reason and give one, before or after the thing it explains.}

Complete TA-C78-for-the-sake-of and answer one why three different ways.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ēṉ]{\ta{ஏன்} (ēṉ) — why}

\label{lesson:TA-C78-why}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}. Then say: I think this is a good house.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஏன்}}
\textbf{\ta{ஏன்}} (\emph{ēṉ}) — \textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{}.

Chapter forty gave you the shape of every Tamil question word: they begin on an \textbf{e-}. \ta{என்ன}, \ta{எங்கே}, \ta{எப்படி}, \ta{எவ்வளவு}. \ta{ஏன்} belongs to the same family, and it is the one that asks for a reason.

It holds a long \textbf{\ta{ஏ}} where the others hold a short \textbf{\ta{எ}}. The family is real; the length is part of this particular member.

On its own it is a whole question:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ஏன்}?} — \textquotedblleft{}Why?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Or in front of a sentence:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ஏன்} \ta{தேநீர்} \ta{வேண்டும்}?} — \textquotedblleft{}Why do you want tea?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

This is the first question in the book that cannot be answered by naming a thing. Its answer is a sentence, and the next lesson is the word that lets you give one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The sixth member of a question family whose pattern you have known since chapter forty.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēṉ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the question words in a row — \emph{eṉṉa, eṅgē, eppaḍi, evvaḷavu, ēṉ}
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{ēṉ tēnīr vēṇḍum?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}, then say \emph{idu nalla vīḍu eṉṟu niṉaikkiṟēṉ}, then ask \emph{ēṉ?}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{pāl vēṇḍumā, alladu tēnīr vēṇḍumā?}, say \emph{nambikkai} and read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}} — three distances back — then ask \ta{ஏன்} about one of them
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āṉāl}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does every Tamil question word begin with, and what is different about this one? (\textbf{An e- — and this one's is long: \ta{ஏ}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ēṉeṉṟāl]{\ta{ஏனென்றால்} (ēṉeṉṟāl) — because}

\label{lesson:TA-C78-because}



\begin{quote}
Give an opinion about a house. Then ask \emph{why}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஏனென்றால்}}
\textbf{\ta{ஏனென்றால்}} (\emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}.

It is long, and it is long for a reason you can already read. Take it apart:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ஏன்}} & \emph{ēṉ} & why — last lesson \\
\textbf{\ta{என்றால்}} & \emph{eṉṟāl} & if it is said \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{"If you ask why —"}. That is the whole word. Tamil answers a \emph{why} by repeating the question and then going on.

\ta{என்றால்} is the same verb you met one chapter ago in \textbf{\ta{என்று}}. There it closed a quotation; here it closes a question and turns it into a hinge.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{தேநீர்} \ta{வேண்டும்}, \ta{ஏனென்றால்} \ta{எனக்குத்} \ta{தாகம்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tēnīr vēṇḍum, ēṉeṉṟāl enakkut tākam.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}I want tea, because I am thirsty.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The second half is a whole sentence — the dative one from chapter six, \emph{to me, thirst}. \ta{ஏனென்றால்} joins it on without changing either side.

Everyday speech shortens it to \textbf{\ta{ஏன்னா}}, the same wearing-down that made \ta{ஆனால்} into \ta{ஆனா}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can ask for a reason and give one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tēnīr vēṇḍum, ēṉeṉṟāl enakkut tākam}
  \item \emph{Split:} say the two halves apart, then join them
  \item \emph{Recall:} say your opinion of a house, then ask \emph{ēṉ?}, then answer with \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{sol}, \emph{paṇivu} and \emph{muṉbu} — three distances back — then ask \ta{ஏன்} about one of them
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{அல்லது}}, then say \emph{sol}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question word is hiding at the front of \ta{ஏனென்றால்}? (\textbf{\ta{ஏன்}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ēṉ]{\ta{ஏன்} — the shortest question in the book}

\label{lesson:TA-W33-read-een}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: ask \emph{why}, then answer with \emph{because}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ஏன்} — two shapes, and one of them is a whole letter}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ஏ}} & \emph{ē} & the free-standing long e, because the word opens on it \\
\textbf{\ta{ன்}} & \emph{ṉ} & \ta{ன} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ஏ} · \ta{ன்} $\to$ \ta{ஏன்}}
\end{quote}

Two shapes. Nothing else in this book is shorter and still a question.

Now set it beside the question word you read in chapter twenty-nine:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எப்படி}} opens on \textbf{\ta{எ}} · \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}} opens on \textbf{\ta{ஏ}}
\end{quote}

Same family, different length, and Tamil gives each length its own letter rather than a mark on one shape. That is why both had to be learnt separately, and why a reader who has both can now tell an \emph{eppaḍi} from an \emph{ēṉ} before hearing either.

The closing \textbf{\ta{ன்}} is the alveolar n you first wrote in chapter seven, the same one that ends \textbf{\ta{நான்}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ஏ}} — then \textbf{\ta{ன்}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}}, then \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}} — long, then short
  \item \emph{Point to:} the two letters that hold the two lengths
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{ēṉ?}, then answer with \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}, then read \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{eṉṟu}, \emph{nel} and \emph{mādam} — three distances back — then ask \ta{ஏன்} about one of them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}}. How does the page tell it apart from \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}}? (\textbf{A different letter for the long e.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[adaṉāl]{\ta{அதனால்} (adaṉāl) — because of that, so}

\label{lesson:TA-C78-therefore}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}}. Then say \emph{because}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அதனால்}}
\textbf{\ta{அதனால்}} (\emph{adaṉāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}because of that\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}so\textquotedblright{}.

\ta{ஏனென்றால்} puts the reason \textbf{after} the result. \ta{அதனால்} puts it \textbf{before}, and points back at it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{எனக்குத்} \ta{தாகம்}. \ta{அதனால்} \ta{தேநீர்} \ta{வேண்டும்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{enakkut tākam. adaṉāl tēnīr vēṇḍum.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}I am thirsty. So I want tea.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same two facts as the last lesson, in the other order. Both are ordinary Tamil, and which one you reach for depends on which half you want to lead with.

The word is \textbf{\ta{அது}} — \textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{}, from chapter forty — carrying an ending that means \emph{by}. \emph{By that.} It can only point backwards, which is why it never opens a conversation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The reason can now go on either side of the result.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{adaṉāl}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enakkut tākam. adaṉāl tēnīr vēṇḍum.}
  \item \emph{Flip:} say the same two facts with \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl} instead
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}, then read \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}}, then say \emph{adaṉāl}
  \item \emph{Return to:} read \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}, say \emph{pul} and say \emph{āṇḍu} — three distances back — then ask \ta{ஏன்} about one of them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two joins puts the reason first? (\textbf{\ta{அதனால்}} — it points back at a reason already given.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-kkāga]{-\ta{க்காக} — what a thing is for}

\label{lesson:TA-C78-for-the-sake-of}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}}. Then say: I am thirsty, so I want tea.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: a reason that is not a sentence}]
\ta{ஏனென்றால்} and \ta{அதனால்} both join a whole sentence. Sometimes the reason is not a sentence at all — it is a person, or a thing.

\textbf{-\ta{க்காக}} (\emph{-kkāga}) is the ending for that. It grows on the dative \textbf{-\ta{உக்கு}} you have had since chapter six.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{with the ending} & \textbf{it means} \\
\midrule
\ta{உங்கள்} & \textbf{\ta{உங்களுக்காக}} & for you \\
\ta{நண்பன்} & \textbf{\ta{நண்பனுக்காக}} & for a friend \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{உங்களுக்காக} \ta{தேநீர்}.} — \emph{uṅgaḷukkāga tēnīr.} — \textquotedblleft{}Tea for you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Hear the \textbf{-\ta{உக்கு}} still inside it. Chapter six taught that ending as \emph{to} or \emph{for}; -\ta{க்காக} sharpens it into \emph{for the sake of}, which is purpose rather than direction.

This is the third answer to \textbf{\ta{ஏன்}} in one chapter: a following sentence, a preceding sentence, and now a single word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A whole chapter about reasons: asking for one, giving one after, giving one before, and naming who a thing is for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{uṅgaḷukkāga}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{uṅgaḷukkāga tēnīr}
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{naṇbaṉukkāga}
  \item \emph{Answer:} ask \emph{ēṉ?} and answer it three ways — with \emph{ēṉeṉṟāl}, with \emph{adaṉāl}, and with \emph{uṅgaḷukkāga}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{payir}, \emph{-um … -um} and \emph{… eṉṟu niṉaikkiṟēṉ} — three distances back — then ask \ta{ஏன்} about one of them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which older ending is inside -\ta{க்காக}? (\textbf{-\ta{உக்கு}}, the dative from chapter six.)
\end{tcolorbox}
